title: Two Sum
statement:
Given an array of integers `nums` and an integer `target`, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to `target`.

You may assume each input has exactly one solution, and you may not use the same element twice. Return the answer in any order.

examples.explanation: nums[0] + nums[1] == 9, so we return [0, 1].
nums[1] + nums[2] == 6.

hints: The brute-force approach checks every pair — that's O(n^2). Can you do it in one pass?
For each number, you need to know if its complement (target - num) has already appeared. What data structure gives O(1) lookups?
Use a hash map from value → index. As you scan, check if the complement is already in the map before inserting the current number.

solution.approach: Walk the array once, keeping a hash map of value → index for numbers already seen. At each element, compute `target - nums[i]`; if that complement is already in the map, you've found your pair — return the stored index and the current index. Otherwise, add `nums[i]` to the map and continue. This trades the O(n^2) brute-force pairwise check for a single O(n) pass with O(1) average lookups.
solution.timeComplexity: O(n) — one pass over the array, O(1) average-case hash map operations.
solution.spaceComplexity: O(n) — the hash map can hold up to n entries.

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
statement:
You're given an array `prices` where `prices[i]` is the price of a stock on day `i`. You want to maximize profit by choosing a single day to buy and a later day to sell.

Return the maximum profit achievable. If no profit is possible, return 0.

examples.explanation: Buy on day 2 (price 1), sell on day 5 (price 6), profit = 6 - 1 = 5.
Prices only fall, so no transaction is profitable — return 0.

hints: Checking every buy/sell pair is O(n^2) — you need a single pass.
As you scan left to right, track the lowest price seen so far — that's your best possible buy point up to this day.
At each day, the best profit if you sold today is `price - minPriceSoFar`. Track the maximum of that across the whole array.

solution.approach: Scan the array once while tracking two running values: the minimum price seen so far (best buy point), and the maximum profit found so far (best sell result). At each day, first update maxProfit using `price - minPrice`, then update minPrice if the current price is lower. This works because by the time you consider selling on day i, minPrice already reflects the best possible buy day before i.
solution.timeComplexity: O(n) — single pass over the array.
solution.spaceComplexity: O(1) — only two running variables.

title: Contains Duplicate
statement: Given an integer array `nums`, return `true` if any value appears **at least twice** in the array, and return `false` if every element is distinct.
hints: Checking every pair for a match is O(n^2) — with up to 10^5 elements that's too slow. You need a way to check 'have I seen this before?' in O(1).
A hash set lets you record numbers as you see them and check membership instantly.
Walk the array once: if the current number is already in the set, return true immediately; otherwise add it. If you finish the loop, return false.

solution.approach: Use a hash set to track numbers seen so far. For each number, check whether it's already in the set — if so, a duplicate exists and we can return true immediately without scanning the rest. Otherwise add it to the set and continue. Since set membership checks and insertions are O(1) on average, this turns the O(n^2) brute-force comparison into a single O(n) pass.
solution.timeComplexity: O(n) — one pass, O(1) average set operations.
solution.spaceComplexity: O(n) — the set can hold up to n elements.

title: Product of Array Except Self
statement:
Given an integer array `nums`, return an array `answer` such that `answer[i]` is equal to the product of all the elements of `nums` except `nums[i]`.

You must write an algorithm that runs in O(n) time and **without using the division operator**.
constraints: The product of any prefix or suffix of nums is guaranteed to fit in a 32-bit integer.
hints: The obvious approach divides the total product by nums[i] — but that breaks when there's a zero in the array, and the problem forbids division anyway.
answer[i] is just (product of everything to the left of i) times (product of everything to the right of i). Can you compute those left and right products separately?

Do one left-to-right pass building prefix products into the answer array, then one right-to-left pass multiplying in suffix products using a running variable — no extra array needed for the suffix pass.

solution.approach: Build the answer in two passes. First, a left-to-right pass fills answer[i] with the product of all elements to the left of i (answer[0] = 1 since there's nothing to the left). Then a right-to-left pass multiplies each answer[i] by the running product of all elements to the right of i, updating that running product as it goes. Combining the two gives, for each index, the product of everything except that index — all without ever dividing, so it handles zeros correctly and runs in O(n) with O(1) extra space beyond the output array.
solution.timeComplexity: O(n) — two linear passes over the array.
solution.spaceComplexity: O(1) extra space — not counting the output array.

title: Maximum Subarray (Kadane's)
statement: Given an integer array `nums`, find the contiguous subarray (containing at least one number) which has the largest sum, and return its sum.

examples.explanation: The subarray [4,-1,2,1] has the largest sum 6.

hints: Checking every possible subarray's sum is O(n^2) or worse. Think about extending a running subarray as you scan left to right.
At each position, decide: does extending the previous subarray with this element help, or is this element better off starting a fresh subarray on its own?
This is Kadane's algorithm: keep a running 'best sum ending here' that resets to just the current element whenever the running sum would drop below it; track the overall maximum as you go.

solution.approach: This is Kadane's algorithm. Track `currentSum`, the best sum of a subarray ending exactly at the current index. At each element, `currentSum` is either the element alone, or the element appended to the previous `currentSum` — whichever is larger; if the previous running sum was negative, it can only drag the total down, so it's better to start fresh at the current element. Track the maximum `currentSum` seen across the whole scan as the answer.
solution.timeComplexity: O(n) — single pass over the array.
solution.spaceComplexity: O(1) — two running variables.

title: Maximum Product Subarray
statement:
Given an integer array `nums`, find a contiguous non-empty subarray within the array that has the largest product, and return the product.

The test cases are generated so that the answer will fit in a 32-bit integer.

examples.explanation: [2,3] has the largest product 6.

constraints: The product of any subarray of nums is guaranteed to fit in a 32-bit integer.
hints: Unlike maximum sum, you can't just track the best running product — a large negative product can become the best positive product if multiplied by another negative number later.
At each position, track both the maximum AND minimum product ending here — the minimum (a very negative number) might become the maximum after multiplying by a negative value.

At each element, compute the three candidates (element alone, element * running max, element * running min), and the new max/min are the largest/smallest of those. Also remember that zeros naturally reset the chain.

solution.approach: Because multiplying by a negative number flips the sign, the most negative running product can suddenly become the most positive one. So instead of tracking only a running maximum (as in Kadane's for sums), track both a running maximum and a running minimum product ending at the current index. At each step, compute the current element times the previous max, times the previous min, and the element alone; the new max and min are the largest and smallest of those three candidates. Track the overall best max seen across the scan. A zero naturally resets both running values to zero (well, to the element itself), so no special-case handling is needed for zeros.
solution.timeComplexity: O(n) — single pass over the array.
solution.spaceComplexity: O(1) — a constant number of running variables.

title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array
statement:
Suppose an array of length n sorted in ascending order is **rotated** between 1 and n times. For example, the array `nums = [0,1,2,4,5,6,7]` might become `[4,5,6,7,0,1,2]` if rotated 4 times.

Given the rotated sorted array `nums`, which contains **no duplicate values**, return the minimum element of the array.

You must write an algorithm that runs in O(log n) time.

examples.explanation: The original array was [1,2,3,4,5] rotated 3 times.
The original array was [0,1,2,4,5,6,7] rotated 4 times.
The array is rotated a full 4 times, so it's still sorted in its original order.

constraints: All the integers of nums are unique.
nums is sorted and rotated between 1 and n times.
hints: A linear scan finds the minimum in O(n), but the array being (partially) sorted hints that binary search can do better — O(log n).
Compare the middle element to the rightmost element. That comparison tells you whether the minimum lies in the left half or the right half.
If nums[mid] > nums[right], the rotation point (and minimum) is somewhere to the right of mid, so search [mid+1, right]. Otherwise the minimum is at mid or to its left, so search [left, mid].

solution.approach: Use binary search, comparing the middle element against the rightmost element of the current search range instead of a fixed target. If `nums[mid] > nums[right]`, the array is 'broken' (the rotation point) somewhere in (mid, right], so the minimum must lie to the right of mid — move `left = mid + 1`. Otherwise, the right half from mid onward is already sorted, meaning the minimum is at mid or somewhere to its left — move `right = mid` (not mid - 1, since mid itself could be the minimum). The loop ends when left == right, which is the index of the minimum.
solution.timeComplexity: O(log n) — binary search halves the range each iteration.
solution.spaceComplexity: O(1) — a few index variables.

title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
statement:
There is an integer array `nums` sorted in ascending order (with **distinct** values), possibly rotated at an unknown pivot. Given the rotated array `nums` and an integer `target`, return the index of `target` if it is in `nums`, or `-1` if it is not.

You must write an algorithm with O(log n) runtime complexity.
constraints: All values of nums are unique.
nums is an ascending array that is possibly rotated.
hints: A plain linear scan works but is O(n) — the sortedness (even though rotated) should let you do O(log n) with binary search.
At any point during binary search, at least one of the two halves [left, mid] or [mid, right] is normally sorted. Figure out which half is sorted first.
Once you know which half is sorted, check whether target falls within that half's value range. If it does, search that half; otherwise, it must be in the other half.

solution.approach: Binary search still works on a rotated sorted array, but with an extra step: at each iteration, at least one of the two halves around `mid` is guaranteed to be normally sorted. Determine which half is sorted by comparing `nums[left]` and `nums[mid]`. If the left half is sorted and target falls within `[nums[left], nums[mid])`, search left; otherwise search right. Symmetrically, if the right half is sorted and target falls within `(nums[mid], nums[right]]`, search right; otherwise search left. This preserves O(log n) despite the rotation.
solution.timeComplexity: O(log n) — binary search, halving the range each step.
solution.spaceComplexity: O(1) — constant extra space.

title: 3Sum
statement:
Given an integer array `nums`, return all the triplets `[nums[i], nums[j], nums[k]]` such that `i != j`, `i != k`, `j != k`, and `nums[i] + nums[j] + nums[k] == 0`.

The solution set must not contain duplicate triplets.

examples.explanation: No triplet sums to 0.

hints: The brute-force triple-nested loop is O(n^3). Sorting the array first opens up a faster way to find pairs that sum to a target.
Fix one number, then the problem reduces to finding two other numbers (in the remaining sorted array) that sum to its negation — a job for the two-pointer technique.

Sort nums. For each index i, use two pointers starting at i+1 and the end of the array, moving inward based on whether the current triplet sum is too small or too large. Skip over duplicate values at every level to avoid duplicate triplets.

solution.approach: Sort the array first. Then fix the first element of the triplet at index i and use the two-pointer technique on the remaining sorted subarray to find pairs summing to `-nums[i]`: start `left` just after i and `right` at the end, and move them inward — if the sum is too small, advance left; if too large, retreat right; if it matches, record the triplet and advance both pointers. Sorting makes duplicate triplets easy to skip: after processing a value at any of the three positions, skip past any repeats of that same value before continuing. This turns the O(n^3) brute force into O(n^2).
solution.timeComplexity: O(n^2) — O(n log n) sort plus an O(n) two-pointer scan for each of n starting indices.
solution.spaceComplexity: O(n) or O(log n) — space for the sorted copy (plus sort's internal space); output space not counted.

title: Container With Most Water
statement:
You are given an integer array `height` of length n. There are n vertical lines drawn such that the two endpoints of the i-th line are `(i, 0)` and `(i, height[i])`.

Find two lines that, together with the x-axis, form a container that holds the most water. Return the maximum amount of water a container can store.

Note that you may not slant the container — the walls are vertical.

examples.explanation: The lines at index 1 (height 8) and index 8 (height 7) form the container with the most water: min(8,7) * (8-1) = 49.

hints: Checking every pair of lines is O(n^2). With up to 10^5 lines, you need a linear approach.
Start with the widest possible container — the two outer walls — and think about which wall you'd ever want to move inward.

Use two pointers at both ends. The water held is limited by the shorter wall, so moving the taller wall inward can only decrease width without any chance of increasing height — always move the pointer at the shorter wall inward.

solution.approach: Start with two pointers at the leftmost and rightmost lines — the widest possible container. At each step, compute the area as `min(height[left], height[right]) * (right - left)` and update the best seen. Then move the pointer at the *shorter* of the two walls inward. This greedy move is safe: keeping the shorter wall in place while shrinking width could never produce a container taller than the current one (it's still capped by the same short wall), so it can only get worse — moving it is the only way to possibly find a taller wall that improves the area. Repeat until the pointers meet.
solution.timeComplexity: O(n) — each pointer moves inward at most n times total.
solution.spaceComplexity: O(1) — a few running variables.

title: Merge Intervals
statement: Given an array of `intervals` where `intervals[i] = [starti, endi]`, merge all overlapping intervals, and return an array of the non-overlapping intervals that cover all the intervals in the input.

examples.explanation: Intervals [1,3] and [2,6] overlap, so they merge into [1,6].
Intervals [1,4] and [4,5] are considered overlapping since they touch at 4.

hints: Comparing every interval against every other is O(n^2). Sorting first can make overlaps easy to spot in a single pass.
If you sort intervals by their start value, any interval that overlaps with the current merged interval must come immediately after it in the sorted order.

Sort by start. Keep a 'current merged interval' — if the next interval's start is <= the current merged interval's end, extend the end (take the max); otherwise close off the current merged interval and start a new one.

solution.approach: Sort the intervals by start value. Then walk through them, maintaining a 'current' merged interval initialized to the first one. For each subsequent interval, if its start is less than or equal to the current interval's end, they overlap (or touch), so extend the current interval's end to the max of the two ends. Otherwise, the current interval can't be extended any further — push it to the result and start a new current interval. Sorting guarantees that any interval overlapping the current one appears immediately next, so a single linear pass after sorting is sufficient.
solution.timeComplexity: O(n log n) — dominated by sorting; the merge pass itself is O(n).
solution.spaceComplexity: O(n) — space for the sorted copy and the result.

title: Insert Interval
statement:
You are given an array of non-overlapping intervals `intervals` where `intervals[i] = [starti, endi]` sorted in ascending order by `starti`, and a new interval `newInterval = [start, end]`.

Insert `newInterval` into `intervals` such that the result is still sorted in ascending order by start and no two intervals overlap (merging overlapping intervals as needed). Return the resulting array of intervals.

examples.explanation: The new interval [4,8] overlaps with [3,5],[6,7],[8,10], merging them into [3,10].

constraints: intervals is sorted by starti in ascending order.
hints: You could append newInterval and re-sort/merge everything, but since intervals is already sorted, you can do this in a single O(n) pass without a full re-sort.

Split the work into three phases as you scan: intervals that end entirely before newInterval starts (copy as-is), intervals that overlap newInterval (merge into it), and intervals that start entirely after newInterval ends (copy as-is).

While the current interval's end is before newInterval's start, just append it. Then while intervals overlap newInterval, grow newInterval's start/end to absorb them. Finally append the (possibly grown) newInterval, then append everything left.

solution.approach: Since the input is already sorted, a single linear pass suffices. First, copy over every interval that ends strictly before `newInterval` starts — they can't overlap it, so they go straight into the result. Next, while the current interval overlaps `newInterval` (its start is <= newInterval's end), absorb it by shrinking newInterval's start to the min and growing its end to the max, then move on. Once no more intervals overlap, push the (possibly expanded) `newInterval` into the result. Finally, copy over all remaining intervals, which by definition start after newInterval ends.
solution.timeComplexity: O(n) — a single linear pass over the intervals.
solution.spaceComplexity: O(n) — for the result array.

title: Next Permutation
statement:
Implement `nextPermutation`, which rearranges numbers into the lexicographically next greater permutation of numbers, in place.

If such an arrangement is not possible (the array is already the highest possible permutation), rearrange it to the lowest possible order (sorted ascending).

The function should mutate the input array in place; for the purposes of this judge, also return the mutated array.

examples.explanation: [3,2,1] is the highest permutation, so it wraps to the lowest, [1,2,3].

hints: The 'next' permutation only changes a suffix of the array. Work from the right end to find where that suffix begins.
Scan from the right to find the first index i where nums[i] < nums[i+1] — that's the 'pivot' that needs to increase. If no such index exists, the whole array is already the last permutation.

After finding the pivot, scan from the right again to find the smallest element to the right of the pivot that's still greater than nums[pivot], swap them, then reverse everything after the pivot's original position to get the smallest possible suffix.

solution.approach: To find the next lexicographic permutation: scan from the right end to find the first index `i` where `nums[i] < nums[i+1]` (the point where the sequence stops being non-increasing from the right). This is the 'pivot' — everything after it is currently the largest possible arrangement of those elements, so it must become the smallest, but first the pivot itself needs to bump up minimally. Find the smallest value to the right of the pivot that is still greater than `nums[i]`, swap it with `nums[i]`, then reverse the whole suffix after position i so it's in ascending (smallest) order. If no such pivot exists (the array is fully non-increasing), the array is already the last permutation, so simply reverse the whole thing to wrap around to the first (smallest) permutation.
solution.timeComplexity: O(n) — a constant number of linear scans over the array.
solution.spaceComplexity: O(1) — mutates the array in place.

title: Set Matrix Zeroes
statement:
Given an m x n integer matrix, if an element is 0, set its entire row and column to 0's. You must do it in place.

For the purposes of this judge, mutate the matrix and also return it.
hints: The naive approach of zeroing rows/columns the moment you see a 0 corrupts the matrix — later checks might see zeros you just wrote rather than the original values. You need to first record where the original zeros are.
You could use a separate set of 'zero rows' and 'zero columns' recorded in a first pass, then apply them in a second pass — that's O(m+n) extra space.

To get O(1) extra space, use the first row and first column of the matrix itself as the marker storage for which rows/columns need zeroing — just remember to track separately whether the first row/column originally contained a zero, since you're about to overwrite it.

solution.approach: First scan the matrix to record, for each row and column, whether it contains a zero — instead of a separate array, use the first row and first column of the matrix itself as marker storage (this achieves O(1) extra space). Since that overwrites matrix[0][0] to double as both a row and column marker, track separately whether row 0 and column 0 originally contained a zero. After marking, do a second pass over the interior of the matrix (excluding row 0 and column 0) and zero out any cell whose row-marker or column-marker is set. Finally, zero out row 0 and/or column 0 themselves if they originally contained a zero.
solution.timeComplexity: O(m*n) — a constant number of passes over the matrix.
solution.spaceComplexity: O(1) — markers are stored in the matrix's own first row/column.

title: Spiral Matrix
statement: Given an m x n `matrix`, return all elements of the matrix in spiral order (starting from the top-left, moving right, then down, then left, then up, and so on inward).
hints: You could simulate a walker turning at boundaries, but it's easy to mess up when to turn. A cleaner way: peel the matrix like an onion, layer by layer.

Maintain four boundaries — top, bottom, left, right rows/columns. Traverse the top row left-to-right, the right column top-to-bottom, the bottom row right-to-left, and the left column bottom-to-top, then shrink all four boundaries inward.

After traversing each of the four sides, immediately check if the boundaries have crossed (e.g. top > bottom) before doing the next side — this prevents re-visiting or fabricating cells in single-row or single-column matrices.

solution.approach: Maintain four shrinking boundaries: top, bottom, left, right. Repeatedly traverse the current top row left-to-right, the current right column top-to-bottom, the current bottom row right-to-left, and the current left column bottom-to-top, tightening the corresponding boundary inward after each side. Crucially, check after each side whether the boundaries have crossed (e.g., `top > bottom` or `left > right`) before doing the next side — this guards against double-counting or fabricating elements when the remaining region collapses to a single row or column. Continue until top exceeds bottom or left exceeds right.
solution.timeComplexity: O(m*n) — every cell is visited exactly once.
solution.spaceComplexity: O(1) extra space — not counting the output array.

title: Rotate Image
statement:
You are given an n x n 2D `matrix` representing an image. Rotate the image by 90 degrees clockwise, in place.

You have to rotate the image without allocating another 2D matrix. For the purposes of this judge, mutate the matrix and also return it.
hints: Rotating into a brand-new matrix is easy, but the problem wants it done in place with no extra 2D array.
A 90-degree clockwise rotation can be decomposed into two simpler, well-known in-place operations performed back to back.
First transpose the matrix (swap matrix[i][j] with matrix[j][i] across the diagonal), then reverse each row. That combination is exactly a 90-degree clockwise rotation.

solution.approach: A 90-degree clockwise rotation is equivalent to first transposing the matrix (reflecting across the main diagonal, so `matrix[i][j]` and `matrix[j][i]` swap) and then reversing each row. Both operations can be done fully in place: the transpose only needs to swap the upper triangle with the lower triangle once each, and reversing a row is a simple two-pointer swap. Doing both in sequence achieves the rotation without allocating a second matrix.
solution.timeComplexity: O(n^2) — every cell is touched a constant number of times.
solution.spaceComplexity: O(1) — rotates in place.

title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
statement: Given a string `s`, find the length of the longest substring without repeating characters.

examples.explanation: The answer is "abc", with length 3.
The answer is "b", with length 1.
The answer is "wke", with length 3. Note that the answer must be a substring; "pwke" is a subsequence, not a substring.

constraints: s consists of English letters, digits, symbols and spaces.
hints: Checking every substring for repeats is O(n^2) or worse. Think about maintaining a 'window' of characters that grows and shrinks as you scan.
Use a sliding window with a hash map/set tracking the last-seen index of each character. When you see a repeat inside the current window, you need to shrink the window from the left.
Keep a window [left, right]. When s[right] is already in the window (its last seen index >= left), move left to one past that character's previous position. Track the max window size seen.

solution.approach: Use a sliding window over the string with a hash map tracking the most recent index at which each character was seen. Expand the window by moving `right` forward one character at a time. If the character at `right` was already seen at an index within the current window (i.e., `>= left`), jump `left` forward to just past that previous occurrence, collapsing the window so it no longer contains a duplicate. At every step, update the running max with the current window size `right - left + 1`. Each character is visited a constant number of times, giving O(n).
solution.timeComplexity: O(n) — each character is processed a constant number of times.
solution.spaceComplexity: O(min(n, charset size)) — the map holds at most one entry per distinct character.

title: Longest Repeating Character Replacement
statement:
You are given a string `s` consisting of only uppercase English letters and an integer `k`. You can choose up to `k` characters of the string and replace them with any other uppercase English letter.

Return the length of the longest substring containing the same letter you can get after performing at most `k` replacements.

examples.explanation: Replace the two 'A's (or two 'B's) with the other letter to get "AAAA" or "BBBB".
Replace one 'A' in the substring "ABAB" with 'B' to get a run of 4 identical letters.

constraints: s consists of only uppercase English letters.
hints: Trying every substring and simulating replacements is far too slow. Think in terms of a sliding window whose validity you can check cheaply.
A window [left, right] is 'achievable' with at most k replacements if (window length) - (count of its most frequent character) <= k — that's how many characters would need to change.

Slide right forward, tracking character counts in the window. Whenever (windowLength - maxFreqInWindow) exceeds k, shrink from the left. The window's length at the end of the scan (tracked as a running max) is the answer.

solution.approach: Use a sliding window [left, right] together with a frequency count of characters inside it. A window is achievable with at most k replacements exactly when `(window length) - (count of the most frequent character in the window)` is <= k — that difference is precisely how many characters would need to be swapped out. Expand right one step at a time, updating counts and the running max frequency seen so far in any window position. If the window becomes invalid (the difference exceeds k), shrink it by moving left forward one step. Because the window only needs to represent the best length found, it never actually needs to shrink below its previous maximum size — so the largest window length seen during the scan is the answer.
solution.timeComplexity: O(n) — each character enters and leaves the window at most once.
solution.spaceComplexity: O(1) — at most 26 uppercase letters tracked in the count map.

title: Minimum Window Substring
statement:
Given two strings `s` and `t`, return the minimum window substring of `s` such that every character in `t` (including duplicates) is included in the window. If there is no such substring, return the empty string `""`.

The test cases are generated such that the answer is unique when it exists.

examples.explanation: The minimum window substring "BANC" includes 'A', 'B', and 'C' from t.
Both 'a's from t must be included, but s only has one 'a', so no valid window exists.

constraints: s and t consist of uppercase and lowercase English letters.
hints: Checking every substring of s against t's requirements is far too slow for the given constraints. A sliding window that grows and shrinks is the way to go.

Track how many of each character t needs (a frequency map), and how many of those requirements are currently satisfied by the window. Expand the window until it satisfies all requirements, then try to shrink it from the left while it still does.

Expand right until the window contains all of t's characters (with correct multiplicities). Then greedily shrink from the left as far as possible while the window remains valid, recording the window whenever it's the smallest valid one seen. Repeat expand/shrink until right reaches the end of s.

solution.approach: Build a frequency map of the characters required by `t`. Use a sliding window [left, right] over `s`, expanding `right` and maintaining a count of how many of `t`'s required characters are currently 'satisfied' (their count in the window reaches their required count). Once the window satisfies all requirements (satisfied count equals the number of distinct characters in t), greedily shrink from the left as far as possible while it remains valid, recording the smallest valid window found along the way. After shrinking as far as possible, continue expanding right. This ensures each character is added and removed from the window a bounded number of times, giving linear time overall.
solution.timeComplexity: O(|s| + |t|) — each character of s is added and removed from the window at most once.
solution.spaceComplexity: O(|s| + |t|) — for the frequency maps (bounded by charset size in practice).

title: Valid Anagram
statement:
Given two strings `s` and `t`, return `true` if `t` is an anagram of `s`, and `false` otherwise.

An anagram is a word or phrase formed by rearranging the letters of a different word or phrase, using all the original letters exactly once.
constraints: s and t consist of lowercase English letters.
hints: Sorting both strings and comparing works but costs O(n log n). Can you verify an anagram in linear time instead?
Two strings are anagrams exactly when they have the same character frequency counts. A hash map (or a fixed-size array for lowercase letters) can track that.
Different lengths can never be anagrams — check that first. Then count characters in s (increment) and t (decrement) into the same map; if every count ends at zero, it's an anagram.

solution.approach: Two strings are anagrams of each other exactly when they contain the same characters with the same frequencies. First check lengths — different lengths can never be anagrams. Then build a single frequency map: increment the count for each character seen in `s`, and decrement for each character seen in `t`. If the strings are true anagrams, every count nets out to zero; if any count is non-zero at the end, they're not anagrams.
solution.timeComplexity: O(n) — linear passes over both strings.
solution.spaceComplexity: O(1) — at most 26 lowercase letters tracked in the map.

title: Group Anagrams
statement: Given an array of strings `strs`, group the anagrams together. You can return the answer in any order (the judge for this problem expects groups in the order each anagram class first appears in `strs`, with strings inside each group kept in their original relative order).
constraints: strs[i] consists of lowercase English letters.
hints: Comparing every pair of strings to check if they're anagrams is O(n^2 * k). You need a way to bucket strings by 'anagram identity' directly.
Two strings are anagrams if and only if they produce the same result when their characters are sorted — that sorted string is a natural grouping key.
Use a hash map from 'sorted characters of the string' to the list of original strings sharing that key. One pass to build the map, then collect its values in insertion order.

solution.approach: Anagrams share a common signature: sorting the characters of any anagram of a word produces the same string. Use a hash map keyed by each string's sorted-character form; for each string in the input, compute this key and append the original string to the map's list for that key (creating the list on first use). A `Map` preserves insertion order, so collecting `map.values()` at the end naturally groups strings in the order their anagram class first appeared.
solution.timeComplexity: O(n * k log k) — n strings, each sorted in O(k log k) where k is its length.
solution.spaceComplexity: O(n * k) — storing all strings, grouped, in the map.

title: Valid Palindrome
statement:
A phrase is a **palindrome** if, after converting all uppercase letters into lowercase letters and removing all non-alphanumeric characters, it reads the same forward and backward.

Given a string `s`, return `true` if it is a palindrome, or `false` otherwise.

examples.input: s = "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama"
examples.explanation: "amanaplanacanalpanama" is a palindrome.
"raceacar" is not a palindrome.
After removing non-alphanumeric characters, s is an empty string, which reads the same forward and backward.

constraints: s consists only of printable ASCII characters.
hints: Building a cleaned copy of the string and comparing it to its reverse works, but you can avoid the extra pass by checking as you go.
Two pointers, one from each end, moving inward, is a natural fit for palindrome checks.

Move the left pointer right (and the right pointer left) past any non-alphanumeric characters, then compare the lowercase versions of what's left. Mismatch means not a palindrome; pointers crossing means it is one.

solution.approach: Use two pointers starting at each end of the string, moving inward. At each step, skip past any character that isn't alphanumeric by advancing the corresponding pointer. Once both pointers rest on alphanumeric characters, compare their lowercase forms — if they differ, the string isn't a palindrome. If they match, move both pointers inward and continue. If the pointers meet or cross without ever finding a mismatch, the string is a palindrome. This avoids allocating a cleaned copy of the string.
solution.timeComplexity: O(n) — each pointer moves inward at most n times total.
solution.spaceComplexity: O(1) — no extra copy of the string is made.

args: A man, a plan, a canal: Panama

title: Longest Palindromic Substring
statement:
Given a string `s`, return the longest palindromic substring in `s`.

If there are multiple longest palindromic substrings of the same length, this judge expects the one found first when expanding outward from every possible center, scanning centers left to right.

examples.explanation: "aba" is also a valid palindrome of the same length, but "bab" is found first when scanning centers left to right.

constraints: s consists of only digits and English letters.
hints: Checking every substring for being a palindrome is O(n^3). There's a smarter way that exploits how palindromes are built from their center outward.
Every palindrome has a center (a single character for odd length, or a gap between two characters for even length). What if you tried expanding outward from every possible center?

For each of the 2n-1 possible centers, expand outward while the characters on both sides match, tracking the longest palindrome found. This is the 'expand around center' technique — O(n^2) time, O(1) space.

solution.approach: Every palindrome is symmetric around some center — either a single character (odd length) or the gap between two adjacent characters (even length). There are `2n - 1` such centers in a string of length n. For each center, expand outward step by step while the characters on both sides match, and track the longest palindrome found so far, only updating when a strictly longer one is found (which naturally keeps the first-found substring in the event of a tie). This 'expand around center' approach checks all possible palindromes in O(n^2) time using only O(1) extra space, avoiding the O(n^3) cost of testing every substring independently.
solution.timeComplexity: O(n^2) — n centers, each expansion can take O(n) in the worst case.
solution.spaceComplexity: O(1) — only a few tracking variables, no extra data structures.

title: Palindromic Substrings
statement:
Given a string `s`, return the number of palindromic substrings in it.

A substring is a contiguous sequence of characters within the string. A string is a palindrome when it reads the same backward as forward.

Substrings with different start or end indices are counted as different substrings even if they consist of the same characters.

examples.explanation: Three palindromic substrings: "a", "b", "c".
Six palindromic substrings: "a", "a", "a", "aa", "aa", "aaa".

constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters.
hints: Testing every one of the O(n^2) substrings for being a palindrome independently costs O(n^3) total. The center-expansion idea from finding the longest palindrome applies here too, just counting instead of tracking the longest.
Every palindrome expands outward from some center — a single character (odd length) or a gap between two characters (even length). There are 2n-1 such centers.

For each of the 2n-1 centers, expand outward while the characters match, and count one palindrome for every successful expansion step — each successful step corresponds to exactly one distinct palindromic substring.

solution.approach: Just like finding the longest palindromic substring, every palindrome is centered either on a single character (odd length) or a gap between two characters (even length), giving `2n - 1` possible centers. For each center, expand outward one step at a time while the two sides match; every successful step (including the initial single-character or two-character check) represents one more distinct palindromic substring, so increment a counter each time the expansion succeeds. Summing this count across all centers gives the total number of palindromic substrings in O(n^2) time.
solution.timeComplexity: O(n^2) — n centers, each expansion can take O(n) in the worst case.
solution.spaceComplexity: O(1) — only a running counter and index variables.
